newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke in pre-emptive strike on Labour spending.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke in pre-emptive strike on Labour spending.

text.p: Britain's Conservative finance minister Kenneth Clarke launched a fierce attack on the opposition Labour party's spending plans on Friday, calling them "a slippery mixture of deception and evasion."

Pre-empting a key speech on the public finances by Labour's finance spokesman Gordon Brown next Monday, Clarke said Labour's spending commitments already totalled 30 billion pounds -- a charge repeatedly denied by the opposition.

"The shape of Gordon Brown's electoral strategy on tax and spending is now becoming clear," Clarke, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, told Conservatives in Lichfield. "It will be a slippery mixture of deception and evasion."
"Labour's worst failure is their artful evasion. They still refuse to reveal their tax plans...Labour's evasion on spending is just as striking."
Brown will deliver a speech entitled "Responsibility in Public Spending" in London on Monday afternoon, the first of what the party is billing as four major addresses on economic policy.

Labour has a strong lead over the Conservatives in opinion polls and looks set to take power in an election due by May 22, but which could take place sooner as the government is now in a minority in parliament.
After nearly 18 years in opposition, the party has worked hard to present a new moderate image and convince voters that its days as the party of high taxation are over.
It has avoided making detailed spending commitments but insisted all its proposals are properly funded.

Labour's main pledges include cutting class sizes in primary schools, reducing waiting lists in the National Health Service by treating an extra 100,000 patients and getting 250,000 under 25-year-olds off unemployment benefit and into work.
The party also pledges fundamental reform of the welfare state but says much of this can be done by using existing resources more efficiently.
Brown has promised "iron discipline" in public spending while party leader Tony Blair said last week that nothing in Labour's programme implied increases in personal taxation.
"There are no uncosted or unfunded spending proposals," Blair said.
But Clarke challenged Labour to come clean about its tax and spending plans.
"Tony Blair and Gordon Brown refuse to face the fact that their front-bench spokesmen have already run up spending commitments totalling 30 billion pounds," he said.

"Either these are spending commitments or they are not. Either they are to be paid for or they have to be given up. Yet Labour will neither explain how their policies are to be financed nor back down from any of them."
